Antibiotics if sputum is purulent or pneumonia (amoxicillin, doxycycline or co-amoxiclav).
Amoxicillin-clavulanate (or ampicillin-sulbactam), or clindamycin; benzylpenicillin plus metronidazole is a traditional alternative.
A bedridden patient with a right lower‑lobe cavity and foul sputum is started on amoxicillin‑clavulanate.
Ciprofloxacin and doxycycline are contraindicated in pregnancy, co-trimoxazole is avoided in the first trimester (folate antagonist), and amoxicillin-clavulanate does not cover MRSA.

qs.q: A patient with uncomplicated community-acquired pneumonia is prescribed oral amoxicillin 500 mg 8-hourly. If the patient has a documented penicillin allergy, which alternative oral antibiotic regimen is recommended?
qs.e: For penicillin-allergic patients with uncomplicated CAP, clarithromycin 500 mg 12-hourly or erythromycin 500 mg 6-hourly is recommended. Co-amoxiclav and ceftriaxone contain beta-lactam rings that may cross-react in penicillin allergies.

qs.q: Your 23-year-old female patient is pregnant and has gonorrhea. The past medical history includes anaphylaxis following exposure to amoxicillin. Worried about compliance, you would like to treat this patient with a single dose, so you chose
qs.e: Spectinomycin is an aminocyclitol antibiotic that can be given as a single intramuscular dose for gonorrhea. It has no cross-reactivity with penicillins (safe in penicillin allergy) and is safe in pregnancy. Ceftriaxone and cefixime have potential cross-reactivity with penicillins. Ciprofloxacin and tetracycline are contraindicated in pregnancy.

ai.subject: Pharmacology
ai.summary: Amoxicillin is a first‑line β‑lactam for common infections in East Africa. Clinicians must recognise its spectrum, resistance patterns, dosing schedules, and avoid misuse that leads to treatment failure.

sections.p: Amoxicillin is a broad‑spectrum penicillin derivative that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis. It is used empirically for respiratory, urinary, skin, and dental infections.
b: Broad spectrum against gram‑positive and many gram‑negative organisms
Requires no renal dose adjustment in most cases

sections.p: Infections treated with amoxicillin are staged by clinical severity: mild (e.g., uncomplicated sore throat), moderate (e.g., community‑acquired pneumonia), severe (e.g., sepsis).
Common pathogens in East Africa that respond to amoxicillin include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus aureus (non‑MRSA), and many enteric bacteria.
Patients present with typical infection signs: fever, localized pain, purulent drainage, or respiratory distress. In low‑resource settings, delayed presentation is common.
Lab and imaging confirm diagnosis and guide therapy. In many rural hospitals, basic tests are limited; clinical judgment is paramount.

t.b: Infiltrate = treat; normal = consider other causes

sections.p: Watch for signs of treatment failure or severe disease: persistent fever, hypotension, altered mental status, or worsening pain.
b: Severe sepsis – immediate IV antibiotics and fluids

sections.p: Treat the infection with amoxicillin, adjusting dose for weight and renal function. Monitor for efficacy and adverse effects.
Re‑evaluate after 48–72 hours; ensure adherence. Prevent resistance by limiting unnecessary prescriptions and ensuring full courses.
b: Educate patients on completing the course

sections.p: Amoxicillin is often mistaken for amoxicillin‑clavulanate; the latter adds β‑lactamase inhibition and broader coverage.
Low sensitivity of rapid strep tests in some settings can give false negatives; clinical judgment remains essential.
b: False negative rapid strep – still treat if high clinical suspicion

faq.q: Can amoxicillin be used in pregnancy?
faq.a: Yes, it is safe in all trimesters and preferred over tetracyclines.

faq.q: What if a patient has a penicillin allergy?
faq.a: Use a non‑penicillin β‑lactam such as cephalexin or a macrolide if no cross‑reactivity.

exam: A 7‑year‑old boy with sore throat and fever: what is the first test and why? — Rapid strep test to confirm bacterial etiology before starting amoxicillin.
A 45‑year‑old woman with pneumonia and purulent sputum: why choose amoxicillin over doxycycline? — Amoxicillin covers common CAP pathogens; doxycycline is reserved for atypical organisms.
A patient develops a rash after 2 days of amoxicillin: what is the next step? — Stop the drug, assess for anaphylaxis, and consider alternative antibiotics.
A child with a urinary tract infection has a negative urine dipstick but high CRP: what should you do? — Repeat urine culture or consider non‑urinary source; high CRP suggests bacterial infection.
A pregnant woman in her first trimester needs antibiotics for dental abscess: which drug is safest? — Amoxicillin is safe; avoid tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones.
A patient with suspected meningitis is started on amoxicillin: why is this inadequate? — Amoxicillin does not penetrate the CSF; use ceftriaxone or vancomycin instead.
